# Diṭṭhi Saṁyutta (SN 24)

**ID:** SN 24  
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Diṭṭhi Saṁyutta  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0303m.mul2.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0303m.mul2.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The central teaching of the saṁyutta is that all speculative views and heresies arise conditioned by grasping and clinging to the five aggregates or empirical personality (*sakkāya*) [Bodhi 2003; Hazra 1994; Perez-Remon 1980]. Employing a structured question-and-answer format, the Buddha addresses a wide spectrum of views, ranging from determinism and moral skepticism to classic cosmological tenets concerning whether the world or the soul is eternal, finite, or distinct from the body [Bodhi 2003; Perez-Remon 1980]. Notably, the opening discourse (SN 24.1, *Vātasutta*) presents a unique philosophical stance asserting that winds do not blow, rivers do not flow, and all things remain immovably fixed like a pillar (*esikaṭṭhāyiṭṭhita*)—a doctrine denying the reality of change affiliated with Pakudha Kaccāyana and early Ājīvikism [Bodhi 2003; Perez-Remon 1980]. Views are further shown to arise from clinging to things perceived, searched for, and pondered over by the mind (*manasā*) [Devdas 2004].

**Sources**

- [Bodhi 2003] Bhikkhu Bodhi, The Connected Discourses of the Buddha: A Translation of the Saṁyutta Nikāya (2000/2003) — Discussed canonical placement, four gamana cycles, relationship to Khandhasamyutta, and note on the static view in SN 24.1.
- [Hazra 1994] Kanai Lal Hazra, Pāli Language and Literature (1994) — Noted the derivation of speculative views from clinging to the five khandhas.
- [Perez-Remon 1980] Joaquin Perez-Remon, Self and Non-Self in Early Buddhism (1980) — Analyzed sakkāya as the root of ditthis and quoted SN 24.1.
- [Devdas 2004] Nalini Devdas, A Study of Cetanā and the Dynamics of Volition in Theravāda Buddhism (Ph.D. thesis, 2004) — Cited PTS reference (S. III. 204–216) and mental pondering (manasā) underlying views.
